questions.q: Why does the segmentation plan deploy in monitor-only (log-only) mode before switching to enforcement?
options: Monitor-only mode is a permanent configuration, and enforcement is never actually turned on
So undocumented legitimate dependencies, like a vendor maintenance tool or a monitoring agent, surface as logged events and can be fixed before enforcement would break them
Because the firewall vendor requires a mandatory trial period
To reduce the cost of the firewall license
questions.explain: Running new deny rules in log-only mode for an observation window surfaces real, previously unnoticed dependencies as logged events, turning them into planned fixes instead of production outages.

questions.q: What two real dependencies did the monitor-only observation window surface?
options: A printer and a guest Wi-Fi network
A vendor's remote maintenance tool reaching the SCADA gateway from outside the jump zone, and an OT monitoring agent polling a corporate logging server outside the allow-listed path
Two unrelated issues with Hartwell's billing system
No dependencies were found; the window was purely a formality
questions.explain: Both were legitimate but undocumented traffic paths — the vendor tool's access was rerouted through the jump zone, and the monitoring agent's path was corrected rather than simply allow-listed as an exception.

questions.q: After enforcement goes live, what do the three connectivity tests in this lesson confirm, and what result should each produce?
options: That all traffic to the SCADA gateway is blocked, with no exceptions
That the jump zone can reach the gateway on 443 (reachable), that an unneeded port on that same path is still blocked, and that corporate IT cannot reach the gateway directly (blocked)
That every zone can reach every other zone equally
Only that the firewall hardware is powered on
questions.explain: The tests check the one intended path works, an unneeded port on that path is still blocked, and the corporate zone that should never reach SCADA directly is in fact blocked — all three must match expectation.

questions.q: Why is the rollback plan written before the maintenance window instead of during it?
options: It isn't actually necessary to write it down at all
So that if enforcement breaks a missed dependency, the team reverts to a pre-defined log-only state calmly, rather than improvising an emergency fix live during an actual OT outage
Because rollback plans are only required for AWS changes, not Azure
To delay the rollout as long as possible
questions.explain: A pre-written rollback trigger and procedure means a missed dependency gets handled by reverting to a known-good state calmly, instead of improvising under pressure during a live incident.

questions.q: Which pillar of the target architecture does this lesson's rollout close out?
options: Pillar three, the automated inventory
Pillar one, the segmented OT/IT boundary
Pillar two, the consolidated identity view
A brand-new, previously undefined fourth pillar
questions.explain: This lesson deploys and validates the Lesson 5 network segmentation design, which is pillar one of the target architecture: the OT/IT boundary moving from implicit trust to enforced, explicit allow-listing.
